title: CODONA v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
In Codona v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mrs. Leanne Codona, is a British national who identifies as a Gypsy, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Her case concerned the difficulties faced by Roma and Traveller families in securing accommodation that respects their cultural traditions, specifically the right to live in caravans rather than conventional housing. Mrs. Codona and her extended family had lived in caravans on a site in Bedfordshire from 1997, but faced repeated enforcement actions by the local council for breaching planning regulations. After a series of planning applications, appeals, and legal proceedings, the council ultimately obtained an injunction requiring the family to leave the site. When Mrs. Codona applied for housing as a homeless person, the only accommodation offered was in “bricks and mortar,” which she could not accept due to her cultural aversion to such housing.

The European Court of Human Rights examined her complaint under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found the application inadmissible, holding that Article 8 does not impose a positive obligation on states to provide a specific type of accommodation, such as a caravan site, especially where no such sites are available. The Court reaffirmed that while states must facilitate the Roma and Traveller way of life, this does not extend to creating new caravan sites to meet demand.

This decision is significant as it clarifies the limits of positive obligations under Article 8 regarding accommodation for Roma and Travellers, following the precedent set in Chapman v. the United Kingdom, and highlights the ongoing challenges these communities face in securing culturally appropriate housing in Europe.
